extracted.intended_audience: Current and prospective peer reviewers for The BMJ (medical journal reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for clinicians and researchers who review manuscripts for The BMJ, covering expectations for the content, conduct, and administration of reviews (including open peer review and ethical disclosures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive critique that helps editors assess importance and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: For the best reviews (those that constructively critique the article and help editors assess its importance and originality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ values reviews that are constructive and that help editors judge a manuscript’s importance and originality; in partnership with the Cleveland Clinic Foundation, particularly good reviews are eligible for up to 3 AMA PRA Category 1 Continuing Medical Education (CME) points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open (signed) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ uses open peer review: reviewers must sign their reports, saying briefly who they are and where they work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must also declare to the editors any competing interests that might relate to articles they are asked to review. Open peer review does not permit authors to contact reviewers directly about reports; all queries should go through the editorial office. If reviewers experience adverse events from open peer review they may contact papersadmin@bmj.com.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to declare any competing interests that might relate to articles they have been asked to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaration is required as part of open peer review and should cover any financial or non-financial interests that could influence the review; see BMJ transparency policy for further details and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise manuscripts according to BMJ’s aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should help prioritise manuscripts bearing in mind that The BMJ aims to publish original, important, and reliable articles that will help readers (mainly doctors) make better decisions about practice, policy, education, and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a manuscript, consider its originality, importance, and reliability and whether it will materially help clinicians, policymakers, educators, or researchers. Note that all research in The BMJ is published open access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to review invitations via the online editorial office
rubrics_metrics.description: When invited to review, reviewers will be emailed and are asked to accept or reject the invitation using The BMJ’s online editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely acceptance or declination through the online system helps editorial triage and allocation of manuscripts to appropriate reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement that reviews may be transferred within BMJ journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can nominate other BMJ journals to receive their manuscript automatically if rejected by the first journal; the system passes on editors' comments and peer reviewers' reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A review written for The BMJ may later be seen by other editors within the BMJ Group; reviewers should be aware their reports can be shared across BMJ journals for editorial use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers advise; editors make the final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers’ role is to advise the editors, who are responsible for the final decision to accept or reject a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews inform but do not determine the editorial decision; provide clear, evidence-based recommendations and reasoning to aid editors’ judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-reviewer process and post-decision sharing of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts sent for review are usually seen by at least two reviewers, and reviewers can access each other's reports on the same manuscript once The BMJ has made its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharing reports post-decision is intended to provide useful feedback and learning; reviewers should write clear reports that can be educational for peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use BMJ transparency policy for ethical concerns (plagiarism, duplicate publication, fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ transparency policy pulls together editorial policies and advises what to do if reviewers are concerned about ethics aspects of a manuscript or suspect plagiarism, duplicate publication, or scientific fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ethical concerns arise during review, consult the transparency policy and notify the editorial office with specific evidence or suspicions so the editors can investigate according to BMJ procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient reviewers evaluate importance and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to traditional peer review, The BMJ asks patient reviewers for their opinion on the importance and relevance of selected manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patient reviewers are asked to provide a lay perspective on whether the research matters to patients and whether findings are presented in a way that patients would find useful or understandable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide feedback to BMJ about manuscripts or the review process
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ welcomes feedback from reviewers about manuscripts, editorial decisions, or the review process in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers who wish to comment on a manuscript decision or on The BMJ’s review process are encouraged to contact the journal to help improve systems and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article provenance statements on accepted papers
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of accepted articles The BMJ will add a statement explaining the article's provenance, e.g., whether it was commissioned and whether it was externally peer reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible provenance statements include: 'Not commissioned; externally peer reviewed', 'Not commissioned; not externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned; externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned; not externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; externally peer reviewed', and 'Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; not externally peer reviewed'. Reviewers should be aware that their involvement contributes to these classifications.
